previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson, a man with a history of systolic heart failure (EF 15%), atrial fibrillation, hypertension, and alcohol abuse, was admitted with chest pain and dizziness after reporting multiple episodes of AICD firing, which was later ruled out. He had a significant drop in hematocrit from baseline to 26.6%, prompting concern for internal bleeding due to a recent altercation involving abdominal and head trauma. CT scans of the head and abdomen showed no acute hemorrhage. He was transfused one unit of packed red blood cells for symptomatic anemia, with improvement in hemoglobin to 10.8 g/dL by discharge. Chest pain was determined to be musculoskeletal, not cardiac or infectious, and resolved with acetaminophen. Pradaxa was held initially but restarted at discharge due to high thrombotic risk. Alcohol withdrawal was managed supportively, and the patient declined referral to a treatment program. He was discharged home in stable condition with clear instructions to avoid alcohol and seek immediate care after any fall or trauma.

radiology_notes.text:
INDICATION:  ___ male with chest pain.

COMPARISON:  Chest radiograph from ___ and CT chest from ___.

CHEST, AP:  Right ventricular pacemaker/defibrillator courses in expected
position.  Lung volumes remain low, with crowding of bronchovascular markings.
There is increased elevation of the right hemidiaphragm, with adjacent right
lower lobe opacity.  New central venous congestion and increased small
bilateral effusions, right greater than left.  Moderate-to-severe cardiomegaly
persists.  

IMPRESSION:
1.  Congestive heart failure.
2.  Moderate-to-severe cardiomegaly.
3.  Right lower lobe atelectasis, which can be seen with acute pulmonary
embolism.  Please refer to subsequent CT for further details.

INDICATION:  Evaluation of patient with chest pain, hemoptysis, and
tachycardia.

COMPARISON:  CT torso from ___.

TECHNIQUE:  MDCT-acquired axial images were obtained from the thoracic inlet
to the base of the lungs prior to administration of IV contrast.  Following
the administration of 100 mL of Omnipaque nonionic intravenous contrast,
MDCT-acquired axial images were obtained from the thoracic inlet to the base
of the lungs.  1.25- and 5-mm collimated images were prepared and reviewed. 
Multiplanar reformatted images were also prepared and reviewed.

FINDINGS:

CHEST CTA:

Opacification of the pulmonary vasculature demonstrates focal filling defects
in the posterior basal segment pulmonary arteries of the right lower lobe
suggestive of a pulmonary embolus in this region (3:44, 46, 603b:39). 
Otherwise, the remainder of the pulmonary vasculature is without any focal
filling defect to suggest a pulmonary embolus.  

Adjacent to the filling defect in the right posterior basal segment, there is
a focal opacity with a mixture of ground galss and confluent opacities (3:54)
which corresponds anatomically to the area of the pulmonary embolus and
consistent with a pulmonary infarct. 

Otherwise, the remainder of the lungs is clear without any focal opacities. 
Previously visualized small-to-moderate right pleural effusion remains stable.
Previously visualized small left pleural effusion has now resolved.

There is no evidence of right heart strain.  The interventricular septum
remains deviated convexly towards the right ventricle.  The pulmonary artery
does not appear dilated.  Single-lead pacemaker appears in place. Heart
remains stably enlarged. 

The previously visualized right pleural effusion has increased in size. The
previously visualized left pleural effusion has resolved. 

A few prominent mediastinal lymph nodes are visualized and likely reactive.
But there is no hilar, mediastinal, or axillary lymphadenopathy by CT size
criteria.

There are no suspicious lytic or sclerotic osseous lesions.

This study is not tailored for evaluation of subdiaphragmatic structures;
however, the visualized portions of the upper liver, spleen, and kidneys
appear normal.

IMPRESSION:
1.  There is evidence of an acute pulmonary embolism in the posterior basal
segment of the right lower lobe.  Additionally, adjacent opacity in the same
anatomical segment correponds to the pulmonary infarct.  However, there is no
evidence of right heart strain or other pulmonary emboli.
2.  Mild increase in small to moderate right pleural effusion may be due to
the pulmonary embolism.
3.  Stable moderate cardiomegaly.
4.  Resolution of previously seen small left pleural effusion.
